question: In the thermogravimetric tests of oil shale kerogen, what sample mass, heating rates, final temperature and purge-gas flow rate were used?
expect: about 5 mg; 5, 10 and 15 C/min; room temperature to 800 C; purge gas 50 mL/min (protective N2 20 mL/min) (sec. 2.3.2)
trap: the STA test's 10 mg and 10 C/min

[Heat Transfer Enhancement in a Shell-and-Tube Type of Heat Exchanger Using Al2O3/Water Nanofluid]

<document title="Heat Transfer Enhancement in a Shell-and-Tube Type of Heat Exchanger Using Al2O3/Water Nanofluid">
=== page 1 ===
- The working fluid in the shell is initially water, which is subsequently replaced by nanofluid composed of water and 15 nm Al2O3 nanoparticles, while the inner tube walls are kept at a constant temperature.
- The largest increase in heat transfer, 37.83%, occurs at a nanoparticle concentration of 1.25% at mass flow rates of 0.5 kg/s, 0.6 kg/s, and 0.7 kg/s.

=== page 2 ===
- The result of this mixture is called a nanofluid.^21 Nanofluids are composed of solid particles of metallic type, metal oxides, carbon-based nanomaterials such as carbon nanotubes, CNTs, or nonmetallic oxides, of nanometric size (less than 100 nm in diameter), which are dispersed in fluids used as coolants, such as water, ethylene glycol, propylene glycol, R600 refrigerant, or oil.^22 This new fluid is used to improve the performance of thermal devices, such as heat exchangers,^21,23−26 without altering their primary geome-try.^27−29 This use is justified by the low thermal conductivity of traditional refrigerants.^30 The principal reason for this improvement in thermal energy exchange capacity is that this mixture has a combined effect of the properties of the base fluid and the nanoparticles.^31 However, the effectiveness of nanofluids in promoting heat transfer can also be influenced by other factors, such as gravity, Brownian motion, Brownian diffusion, the friction force between the fluid and the nanoparticles, sedimentation, dispersion, and stratification at the solid/liquid interface; these factors may simultaneously interact within the main flow of this fluid.^18 Consequently, several studies have focused on identifying the mechanisms that influence heat transfer in nanofluids while demonstrating that an improvement in thermal conductivity alone is not sufficient to explain the performance gains observed in the process.^32 Nanofluids formulated with Al2O3 nanoparticles have attracted significant attention due to their superior thermal characteristics, high productivity, and stability.^33 For instance, Main et al.^23 investigated the thermal conductivity of trifluoromethylsulfonyl (as base fluid) and the thermal conductivity after the addition of Al2O3 nanoparticles at a 1.0% volumetric concentration, diameters of 10 nm, 30, 60, and 90 nm and varying temperatures (10 °C - 70 °C).
- The results showed that thermal conductivity increased by up to 14.63% when nanoparticles with a diameter of 10 nm were added at 70 °C. Albadr et al.^34 investigated the heat transfer performance of a shell-and-tube heat exchanger operating under counter-current and turbulent flow conditions with Al2O3/distilled water nanofluids.
- Moreover, when the nanoparticle concentration reached 2% by volume, the overall heat transfer coefficient improved by up to 57% compared to that of pure distilled water.
- Another relevant contribution was presented by Oztürk, Tezcan, and Çiftçi,^35 who performed a computational analysis on heat transfer enhancement in a shell-and-tube heat exchanger using Al2O3/water and CNT/water nanofluids at concentrations of 3%, 6%, and 9%.
- The maximum enhancement compared with pure water was approximately 50% and 62.5% at a concentration of 6% for Al2O3/water nanofluids, respectively.
- Although improvements were also observed at 9% concentration, the enhancement was reduced due to the dominant effect of viscosity at higher nanoparticle loadings, which negatively affects heat transfer, as reported in previous studies.^36 Similarly, Gkountas et al.^37 evaluated heat transfer enhance-ment in a supercritical CO2 Brayton cycle printed circuit heat exchanger using an Al2O3/water nanofluid.
- The results showed that a maximum volume fraction of 5% nanoparticles resulted in a 10% improvement in the heat-transfer coefficient compared to pure water.
- This improvement allowed for an additional 0.9% reduction in the length of the heat exchanger, along with a decrease in the pressure drop of up to 14%.
